facts.claim: "Cliffy" is track 4 on Matt Maeson's six-track EP The Hearse, released 2018-04-27 worldwide on Neon Gold/Atlantic. It runs 3:48.
"Cliffy" was written by James Flannigan and Matt Maeson.
Read Dork's song credits list James Flannigan as the producer of "Cliffy".

The lyrics follow a narrator who sees Cliffy cutting close to a power line while Cliffy's father is too high to notice. The narrator says he won't warn them because he is running low and Cliffy is his supply.

Fan accounts say Maeson explains the story behind "Cliffy" from the stage at live shows, for example at Saturn in Birmingham on 3/12/22. His own account of the song's origin was not found in a published interview.
The Hearse EP's lead single was "Hallucinogenics". The Partae's announcement of the EP lists the tracklist, including "Cliffy".
A live version of "Cliffy" appears on Maeson's 2024 release That's My Cue: A Solo Experience.
Maeson released the EP Who Killed Matt Maeson in 2017 and The Hearse in 2018. His debut album Bank on the Funeral followed on April 5, 2019.
Maeson comes from Virginia Beach. His parents played in Christian heavy-metal bands. He grew up travelling with their outreach ministry and performing in prisons and at biker rallies.

Maeson has described falling into drug use and getting arrested repeatedly. He lost about three years to addiction and left his family. Reconciling with them and getting his life in order set his music career in motion.

research.lineage: Maeson is a confessional, darkly honest singer-songwriter in the alternative/indie vein, writing about addiction, redemption and faith, shaped by his prison-ministry and biker-rally upbringing.

draft:
The coldest line in **Cliffy** comes early, and Matt Maeson doesn't dress it up. Cliffy is cutting close to a power line, his father is too high to notice, and the narrator sees all of it and keeps quiet. The reason lands flat as a receipt: "'Cause I'm running real low and he's my supply." It's a confession of the ugliest kind of math, where someone else's safety gets weighed against your own need and loses. Maeson doesn't apologize for it in the verse. He lets it sit there.

Then the chorus turns soft, and the softness is the hard part. "Are you still hurting?" someone asks, wanting to know where all those burdens came from. The lyric never says who's asking. It could be the narrator to Cliffy, voicing a care he couldn't manage when it counted. It could be God, who shows up in the second verse wrestling with the narrator, telling him to quit pulling his hair out and promising he won't be drowned out with alcohol. Or the narrator could be asking himself. Guilt and tenderness share the same melody, and the song doesn't choose between them.

Maeson grew up in Virginia Beach with parents who played in Christian heavy-metal bands. He travelled with their outreach ministry, performing in prisons and at biker rallies. He has talked about losing roughly three years to addiction, getting arrested again and again, leaving his family, and finding his way back to them before the music took off. The song never claims to be autobiography. But its argument with God has the worn-in feel of someone raised to expect an answer, and someone who knows what it means to be a person's supply or to need one. Fans say he tells the story behind it from the stage.

He wrote it with James Flannigan, who also produced, and they kept it plain. Acoustic guitar strums over a walking bass line, and the drums hold a moderate, driving beat. A second voice harmonizes on some phrases and thickens the line. The mix is dry and a little raw, with a room around it, full without crowding Maeson's raspy, unpolished voice. Nothing sands the edges off the confession.

The last new words are a vow, repeated four times: "I bet my life on you." Aimed at God, it's faith. Aimed at Cliffy, the supply, it's the addiction talking. The song lets both readings stand, which is more honest than picking one.

It makes you stand where the narrator stands, close enough to see someone in danger and too needy to speak, and then it asks, gently, whether you're still hurting anyway.
